claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Iglesias-Bartolome et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Oral mucosa shows limited scarring following injury.
claims.source: Despite its similarities to human skin, oral mucosa undergoes faster cellular turnover and shows limited scarring following injury (Iglesias-Bartolome et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Iglesias-Bartolome et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Periodontitis represents the 11th most prevalent worldwide disease.
claims.source: Masticatory mucosa or gingiva (tooth-associated mucosa) is the first structure to be affected by an oral chronic disease – periodontitis, which represents the 11th more prevalent worldwide disease and is highly correlated with the worsening of systemic conditions, such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease (Kinane et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kinane et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Periodontitis is highly correlated with the worsening of systemic conditions such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
claims.source: Masticatory mucosa or gingiva (tooth-associated mucosa) is the first structure to be affected by an oral chronic disease – periodontitis, which represents the 11th more prevalent worldwide disease and is highly correlated with the worsening of systemic conditions, such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease (Kinane et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kinane et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Masticatory mucosa or gingiva is the first structure to be affected by periodontitis.
claims.source: Masticatory mucosa or gingiva (tooth-associated mucosa) is the first structure to be affected by an oral chronic disease – periodontitis, which represents the 11th more prevalent worldwide disease and is highly correlated with the worsening of systemic conditions, such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease (Kinane et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about periodontitis pathogenesis, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Oral mucosa is a highly heterogeneous and complex tissue with dynamic recruitment and expansion and/or depletion of various cell types.
claims.source: Recent studies from our lab and others have described the oral mucosa transcriptional profile demonstrating that it is a highly heterogeneous and complex tissue with dynamic recruitment and expansion and/or depletion of various cell types (Caetano et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2021; Williams et al., 2021)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three studies including the authors' previous work.

claims.claim: Spatial transcriptomic technologies enable untargeted and comprehensive capture of cellular transcriptomic profiles in situ.
claims.source: These tools enable untargeted and comprehensive capture of cellular transcriptomic profiles in situ, and therefore, can overcome limitations of in situ hybridisation (ISH), and allow discoveries of previously undetectable transcriptomic changes.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of spatial transcriptomic technologies based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: Spatial transcriptomic technologies can overcome limitations of in situ hybridisation (ISH).
claims.source: These tools enable untargeted and comprehensive capture of cellular transcriptomic profiles in situ, and therefore, can overcome limitations of in situ hybridisation (ISH), and allow discoveries of previously undetectable transcriptomic changes.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of spatial transcriptomics based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: Physical proximity of cells often reflects relatedness in tissue architecture.
claims.source: The cellular architecture of tissues, where distinct cell types are organised in space, underlies cell–cell communication, organ function, and pathology as physical proximity often reflects relatedness.
claims.evidence: This is a general principle in tissue biology based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: Spatial information of cell transcriptomes provides information about how cells coordinate to perform their biological functions in cell–cell signalling mechanisms.
claims.source: Thus, the spatial information of cell transcriptomes provides information about how cells coordinate to perform their biological functions in cell–cell signalling mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the utility of spatial transcriptomics based on established principles.

claims.claim: Stromal cells play an emerging role in shaping tissue pathology by controlling local immune responses.
claims.source: We characterise a rare immunogenic fibroblast population, which supports our and other studies on the emerging role of stromal cells in shaping tissue pathology by controlling local immune responses (Croft et al., 2019; Davidson et al., 2021; Kinchen et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three studies.

claims.claim: Healthy human oral mucosa samples were analysed by spatial transcriptomics using 10X Genomics Visium.
claims.source: To systematically study the spatial patterns of gene expression of human oral mucosa that we previously described (Caetano et al., 2021) and understand in situ tissue organisation, healthy human oral mucosa samples were analysed by spatial transcriptomics (ST) (10X Genomics Visium) (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claims.claim: Two distinct anatomical locations were used in the analyses: buccal (anterior) and palatal (posterior) from three individuals.
claims.source: Two distinct anatomical locations were used in our analyses – buccal (anterior; Figure 1B–F) and palatal (posterior; Figure 1—figure supplement 1) from three individuals.
claims.evidence: This describes the sample collection strategy used in the study.

claims.claim: 10-µm-thick paraffin and 15-µm-thick cryosection slices from five individual healthy samples in total were analysed.
claims.source: In each experiment, 10-µm-thick paraffin and 15-µm-thick cryosection slices from five individual healthy samples in total were analysed.
claims.evidence: This describes the sample preparation methodology.

claims.claim: Two technical replicates for two biological replicates were generated to understand technical variability and no major differences were detected.
claims.source: We generated two technical replicates for two biological replicates to understand technical variability and no major differences were detected (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This describes experimental validation and results from technical replicates.

claims.claim: Spatial transcriptomics typically captured more than 40,000 mean reads under tissue per spot representing over 2000 genes per 55 µm spot.
claims.source: Typically, this captured more than 40,000 mean reads under tissue per spot representing over 2000 genes per 55 µm spot.
claims.evidence: This describes the sequencing depth and gene detection achieved in the study.

claims.claim: Analyses of transcriptional signatures of ST spots identified between 4 and 10 oral mucosa compartments in each slide.
claims.source: Analyses of transcriptional signatures of ST spots identified between 4 and 10 oral mucosa compartments in each slide, which mapped to distinct locations and allowed us to define anatomical regions from a molecular perspective (Figure 1C–E, Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2, Figure 1—source data 1, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the clustering analysis results with reference to figures.

claims.claim: ST spots measure 55 µm and contain multiple cell types.
claims.source: Since ST spots measure 55 µm, these contain multiple cell types.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the technical limitation of the Visium platform based on manufacturer specifications.

claims.claim: A computational tool was used to deconvolute each spot and predict the underlying composition of cell types.
claims.source: To address this low resolution, we used a new computational tool to deconvolute each spot and predict the underlying composition of cell types (Zhao et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This describes the computational method used, supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2021.

claims.claim: The deconvolution method uses neighbour structure in spatial transcriptomic data to increase the resolution at a subspot level.
claims.source: This method uses neighbour structure in spatial transcriptomic data to increase the resolution at a subspot level and infers from the existing literature for use of Bayesian statistics to achieve high-resolution images.
claims.evidence: This describes the computational approach based on the cited method.

claims.claim: Most cluster regions were distributed in layers, highlighting that the largest determinant of transcriptional/cellular spatial variability corresponds to tissue depth.
claims.source: Most cluster regions were distributed in layers, highlighting that the largest determinant of transcriptional/cellular spatial variability corresponds to tissue depth as described in other barrier organs (Fawkner-Corbett et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the data analysis, supported by comparison to other barrier organs via citation.

claims.claim: KRT1 mapped into the suprabasal epithelial region.
claims.source: We found molecular patterns that mapped into known anatomical areas; for example, KRT1 mapped into the suprabasal epithelial region, and KRT15 into the basal epithelial layer.
claims.evidence: This is a specific finding from the spatial mapping analysis.

claims.claim: KRT15 mapped into the basal epithelial layer.
claims.source: We found molecular patterns that mapped into known anatomical areas; for example, KRT1 mapped into the suprabasal epithelial region, and KRT15 into the basal epithelial layer.
claims.evidence: This is a specific finding from the spatial mapping analysis.

claims.claim: The subepithelial stromal region shows specific GO terms for epidermis development, stem cell differentiation, and morphogenesis of the epithelium.
claims.source: Within the less characterised lamina propria we observed transcriptionally distinct regions with possibly distinct cellular functions; for example, the subepithelial stromal region shows specific GO terms for epidermis development, stem cell differentiation, and morphogenesis of the epithelium, which follows recent research on subepithelial niche areas (Kinchen et al., 2018; Shoshkes-Carmel et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from GO enrichment analysis, supported by citations to related research.

claims.claim: Lower reticular regions show mostly ECM organisation terms.
claims.source: By contrast, lower reticular regions show mostly ECM organisation terms (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from GO enrichment analysis with reference to a figure.

claims.claim: The compartmentalisation of papillary and reticular fibroblasts is known in the skin.
claims.source: These results follow the known compartmentalised of papillary and reticular fibroblasts in the skin (Plikus et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to established knowledge in skin biology, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Tissue from four different patient samples with periodontal disease was analysed by spatial transcriptomics.
claims.source: To understand how tissue organisation is reshaped in disease, we investigated changes in tissue organisation and gene expression in patients with periodontal disease. We again undertook ST (10X Visium) on tissue from four different patient samples.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design for disease samples.

claims.claim: Analyses of transcriptional signatures of ST spots identified between 5 and 10 spot clusters in each disease slide.
claims.source: Analyses of transcriptional signatures of ST spots identified between 5 and 10 spot clusters in each slide, which again mapped to discreet anatomical locations (Figure 2A–E).
claims.evidence: This describes the clustering analysis results for disease samples.

claims.claim: Hallmarks of a pro-inflammatory tissue microenvironment were observed in disease.
claims.source: We readily identified similar cluster regions as detected in healthy mucosa, and we observed hallmarks of a pro-inflammatory tissue microenvironment in disease (Figure 2E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the disease sample analysis with reference to figures.

claims.claim: The spatial patterns of top marker genes matched well with immunohistochemistry results.
claims.source: To validate the spatial transcriptomes that we obtained, we compared spatial expression patterns of top marker genes of oral mucosa tissue with known tissue markers. The spatial patterns of these transcripts matched well with those of immunohistochemistry (IHC) results (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This describes validation of spatial transcriptomics data using IHC.

claims.claim: Several disease-associated changes were observed in the stromal compartment, exemplified by an overall upregulation of pro-inflammatory gene signatures.
claims.source: We also observed several disease-associated changes in the stromal compartment, exemplified by an overall upregulation of pro-inflammatory gene signatures (Figure 2E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—source data 1)
claims.evidence: This is a finding from differential expression analysis with reference to figures.

claims.claim: Upregulation of genes involved in vascular transport (CXCL12) and blood vessel morphogenesis (CLDN5, TAGLN) was observed in disease.
claims.source: We also observed several disease-associated changes in the stromal compartment, exemplified by an overall upregulation of pro-inflammatory gene signatures (Figure 2E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—source data 1), and upregulation of genes involved in vascular transport (CXCL12) and blood vessel morphogenesis (CLDN5, TAGLN) (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is a specific finding from differential expression analysis.

claims.claim: Tissue-specific properties reflect local organisation.
claims.source: These results support the hypothesis that tissue-specific properties reflect local organisation.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the results based on the observed spatial patterns.

claims.claim: CDKN2B, IL1A, IL1B, and VAMP8 specifically localised in the junctional epithelium region.
claims.source: Mapping of 21 known disease genes with our spatial data allowed us to link genotypes with phenotypes that likely manifest through highly cell-type and location-specific defects and result in pathology. From these, CDKN2B, IL1A, IL1B, and VAMP8 specifically localised in the junctional epithelium region (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from mapping GWAS risk genes to spatial data.

claims.claim: Dysfunctional junctional epithelium might be a major driver of periodontal disease pathogenesis.
claims.source: In summary, our analysis suggests that dysfunctional junctional epithelium might be a major driver of periodontal disease pathogenesis.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the spatial localization of disease risk genes.

claims.claim: The gingival epithelium can be divided into three distinct anatomical regions: oral (OE), sulcular (OSE), and junctional epithelium (JE).
claims.source: The most fundamental function of an epithelial tissue is to act as a barrier; the gingival epithelium can be divided into three distinct anatomical regions – oral (OE), sulcular (OSE), and junctional epithelium (JE) (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about gingival epithelium.

claims.claim: In health, the junctional epithelium attaches to the tooth, providing a seal against oral microorganisms.
claims.source: In health, the JE attaches to the tooth, providing a seal against oral microorganisms, thus having a profound role in the innate response.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about junctional epithelium function.

claims.claim: Breakdown of the junctional epithelium attachment results in loss of periodontal ligament, alveolar bone resorption, and often, tooth loss.
claims.source: Breakdown of this attachment results in loss of periodontal ligament, alveolar bone resorption, and often, tooth loss.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about periodontitis pathogenesis.

claims.claim: The analyses were able to unbiasedly distinguish between all three types of epithelia based on their gene expression.
claims.source: Since we were able to collect intact tissues that incorporated the entire gingival margin, our analyses were able to unbiasedly distinguish between all three types of epithelia based on their gene expression (Figure 3A), suggesting that these are transcriptionally distinct.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the spatial transcriptomics analysis.

claims.claim: Oral epithelium is enriched in genes related to integrin-mediated signalling pathway and keratinocyte differentiation.
claims.source: Oral epithelium is enriched in genes related to integrin-mediated signalling pathway and keratinocyte differentiation, whereas both sulcular and junctional epithelia show mostly terms related to immune response (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from GO enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: Both sulcular and junctional epithelia show mostly terms related to immune response.
claims.source: Oral epithelium is enriched in genes related to integrin-mediated signalling pathway and keratinocyte differentiation, whereas both sulcular and junctional epithelia show mostly terms related to immune response (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from GO enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: KRT13 and KRT4 are restricted to the sulcular epithelium.
claims.source: They also show distinct keratin signatures with KRT13 and KRT4 being restricted to the sulcular epithelium and KRT18 specific to the junctional epithelium (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from spatial gene expression mapping.

claims.claim: KRT18 is specific to the junctional epithelium.
claims.source: They also show distinct keratin signatures with KRT13 and KRT4 being restricted to the sulcular epithelium and KRT18 specific to the junctional epithelium (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from spatial gene expression mapping.

claims.claim: SOX9 shows a restricted expression to the junctional epithelium.
claims.source: Interestingly, SOX9 shows a restricted expression to the junctional epithelium, and it is known to be expressed in stem cells/progenitors in several tissues such as gut and skin (Jo et al., 2014), and may label similar populations in the human oral mucosa (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from spatial gene expression mapping, with citation to support SOX9's role in other tissues.

claims.claim: SOX9 is known to be expressed in stem cells/progenitors in several tissues such as gut and skin.
claims.source: Interestingly, SOX9 shows a restricted expression to the junctional epithelium, and it is known to be expressed in stem cells/progenitors in several tissues such as gut and skin (Jo et al., 2014), and may label similar populations in the human oral mucosa (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Jo et al., 2014.

claims.claim: SOX9 may label stem cell/progenitor populations in the human oral mucosa.
claims.source: Interestingly, SOX9 shows a restricted expression to the junctional epithelium, and it is known to be expressed in stem cells/progenitors in several tissues such as gut and skin (Jo et al., 2014), and may label similar populations in the human oral mucosa (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on SOX9's known function in other tissues and its expression pattern in oral mucosa.

claims.claim: The basal proliferative epithelial progenitor layer shows high expression of KRT8, IGFBP2, FOXP2, and NEFM.
claims.source: We also analysed the basal proliferative epithelial progenitor layer, which shows high expression of KRT8, IGFBP2, FOXP2, and NEFM (neurofilament medium chain) (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from spatial gene expression analysis.

claims.claim: A rare disease-associated epithelial proliferative population was identified in the reference dataset, characterised by TOP2A and CENPF expression.
claims.source: Furthermore, in our reference dataset we identified a rare disease-associated epithelial proliferative population characterised by TOP2A and CENPF expression.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq reference dataset.

claims.claim: Expression of TOP2A was highly restricted to the junctional epithelium and significantly increased when compared to healthy samples.
claims.source: When mapped into the spatial data, we observed that expression of TOP2A was highly restricted to the junctional epithelium and significantly increased when compared to healthy samples.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from spatial mapping and comparison between health and disease.

claims.claim: Other proliferation markers were also increased in disease.
claims.source: Other proliferation markers were also increased in disease (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis in disease samples.

claims.claim: An inflammatory environment leads to an increased basal epithelial proliferation.
claims.source: Thus, an inflammatory environment leads to an increased basal epithelial proliferation, suggesting that chronic inflammatory disease may regulate stem cell behaviour.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed increase in proliferation markers in disease.

claims.claim: Chronic inflammatory disease may regulate stem cell behaviour.
claims.source: Thus, an inflammatory environment leads to an increased basal epithelial proliferation, suggesting that chronic inflammatory disease may regulate stem cell behaviour.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed changes in proliferation.

claims.claim: Distinct stromal regions clustered adjacent to the different epithelial regions, suggestive of playing a part in epithelial specification or dysregulation.
claims.source: Furthermore, distinct stromal regions also clustered adjacent to the different epithelial regions similar to healthy samples, suggestive of playing a part in epithelial specification or dysregulation (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from spatial clustering analysis with interpretation.

claims.claim: Within the junctional epithelium area, a distinct pro-inflammatory stromal signature was observed with specific expression of genes involved in 'neutrophil activation' and 'neutrophil degranulation'.
claims.source: Within the junctional epithelium area, we observed a distinct pro-inflammatory stromal signature with specific expression of genes involved in 'neutrophil activation' and 'neutrophil degranulation' (Figure 3D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
claims.evidence: This is a finding from GO enrichment analysis of spatially defined regions.

claims.claim: The stromal sulcular epithelium region showed genes involved in angiogenesis.
claims.source: whereas, the stromal sulcular epithelium region showed genes involved in angiogenesis (Figure 3D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from GO enrichment analysis of spatially defined regions.

claims.claim: In health, dominant interactions were observed between suprabasal and basal epithelial layers (MMP9-LRP1; ADAM17-NOTCH1).
claims.source: Thus, we generated a spatial neighbourhood network (Figure 4A), where in health we observed dominant interactions between suprabasal and basal epithelial layers (MMP9-LRP1; ADAM17-NOTCH1) (Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from cell-cell communication analysis using Giotto.

claims.claim: In disease, the emergence of several stromal region interactions was observed, particularly reticular regions.
claims.source: In disease, we see the emergence of several stromal region interactions, particularly reticular regions (Figure 4A), whereas in health these interactions are downregulated (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from cell-cell communication analysis comparing health and disease.

claims.claim: A downregulation of endothelial–subepithelial interactions was observed in health (VWF-LRP1, MMP9-LRP1).
claims.source: Furthermore, we see a downregulation of endothelial–subepithelial interactions in health (VWF-LRP1, MMP9-LRP1)
claims.evidence: This is a finding from cell-cell communication analysis.

claims.claim: In disease, the junctional epithelium shows pro-inflammatory interactions with the adjacent stroma (NRG1-EGFR, LRIG1-EGFR, TGFA-EGFR).
claims.source: and in disease, the junctional epithelium shows pro-inflammatory interactions with the adjacent stroma (NRG1-EGFR, LRIG1-EGFR, TGFA-EGFR).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from cell-cell communication analysis in disease samples.

claims.claim: Stromal/immune/endothelial interactions are dominant in disease, whereas structural non-immune interactions shape tissue physiology.
claims.source: Collectively, these findings suggest that stromal/immune/endothelial interactions are dominant in disease, whereas structural non-immune interactions shape tissue physiology.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the cell-cell communication analysis results.

claims.claim: The scRNA-seq dataset was integrated with the spatial transcriptome data to localise well-characterised cell types.
claims.source: Upon further examination of the oral mucosa spatial features, clusters revealed high cell type complexity. Thus, to dissect cell type composition, we first integrated our previously generated scRNA-seq dataset with the spatial transcriptome data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the integration methodology used.

claims.claim: Proliferative epithelial cells mapped at the basal epithelial layer.
claims.source: This localised well-characterised cell types, such as proliferative epithelial cells mapped at the basal epithelial layer, and suprabasal keratinocytes in the suprabasal layer.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the integration of scRNA-seq and spatial data.

claims.claim: Suprabasal keratinocytes mapped in the suprabasal layer.
claims.source: This localised well-characterised cell types, such as proliferative epithelial cells mapped at the basal epithelial layer, and suprabasal keratinocytes in the suprabasal layer.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the integration of scRNA-seq and spatial data.

claims.claim: The method accurately maps oral mucosa cell types and was able to detect cell types that went undetected in the reference scRNA-seq dataset, such as melanocytes.
claims.source: We observed that this method accurately maps oral mucosa cell types, and we were able to detect cell types that went undetected in our reference scRNA-seq dataset, such as melanocytes (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the spatial mapping approach.

claims.claim: A substantial increase in endothelial cell expression and distribution was observed in the oral subepithelial and reticular stroma.
claims.source: Importantly, we observed a substantial increase in endothelial cell expression and distribution in the oral subepithelial and reticular stroma, which contradicts our scRNA-seq analysis alone emphasising the need to complement single-cell analyses with other data modalities.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from spatial mapping that differs from scRNA-seq results.

claims.claim: Fine-grained immune cell types that went undetected in the reference dataset were detected, such as γδ T cells and Tregs.
claims.source: Again, we were able to detect fine-grained immune cell types that went undetected in our reference dataset, such as γδ T cells and Tregs (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from spatial mapping of immune cells.

claims.claim: An increase in most immune cell types was observed, particularly of macrophages and γδ T cells.
claims.source: Overall, we observed an increase in most immune cell types, particularly of macrophages and γδ T cells.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from comparing immune cell mapping between health and disease.

claims.claim: γδ T cells were found in sulcular and junctional epithelial regions.
claims.source: The latter were found in sulcular and junctional epithelial regions.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from spatial mapping of γδ T cells.

claims.claim: Flow cytometry studies have reported that there is a significant recruitment of neutrophils in disease.
claims.source: Flow cytometry studies have reported that there is a significant recruitment of neutrophils in disease (Dutzan et al., 2016)
claims.evidence: This is a statement of prior findings supported by citation.

claims.claim: scRNA-seq was insufficient in characterising neutrophils in previous work.
claims.source: however, in our previous work and in subsequent studies (Huang et al., 2021; Williams et al., 2021), scRNA-seq was insufficient in characterising these cells.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about limitations of prior scRNA-seq studies, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Neutrophils were mapped and observed to significantly increase in disease as reported previously.
claims.source: Here, we were able to map these cells and observed a significant increase in disease as reported previously (Dutzan et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from spatial mapping that confirms prior flow cytometry results.

claims.claim: Changes in the immune profile agreed with an initial immune response of a significant infiltration of myeloid cells and lymphocytes.
claims.source: In short, changes in the immune profile agreed with an initial immune response of a significant infiltration of myeloid cells and lymphocytes, and importantly, composition changes also follow changes in spatial distribution.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the immune cell mapping results.

claims.claim: Composition changes also follow changes in spatial distribution.
claims.source: In short, changes in the immune profile agreed with an initial immune response of a significant infiltration of myeloid cells and lymphocytes, and importantly, composition changes also follow changes in spatial distribution.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the spatial analysis.

claims.claim: Five molecularly distinct fibroblast subtypes were identified based on the scRNA-seq reference.
claims.source: To identify regionally enriched fibroblasts, we first annotated and spatially mapped five molecularly distinct fibroblast subtypes that were identified based on our scRNA-seq reference.
claims.evidence: This describes the fibroblast classification from the reference dataset.

claims.claim: Only three of the five fibroblast subtypes mapped into the spatial data.
claims.source: Only three of the five subtypes mapped into our spatial data; therefore, we used BayesSpace to map all subtypes using Seurat differential gene expression markers data (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the spatial mapping of fibroblast subtypes.

claims.claim: Subtypes were identified that were spatially enriched in the reticular (Fb1, Fb3), subepithelial (Fb2), and immune enriched regions (Fb4, Fb5).
claims.source: We identified subtypes that were spatially enriched in the reticular (Fb1, Fb3), subepithelial (Fb2), and immune enriched regions (Fb4, Fb5).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from spatial mapping of fibroblast subtypes.

claims.claim: Fibroblast 2 (GREM1+, SFRP1+) showed an increased spatial enrichment in the subepithelial region compared to the other subtypes.
claims.source: Fibroblast 2 (GREM1+, SFRP1+) showed an increased spatial enrichment in the subepithelial region compared to the other subtypes, and a substantial enrichment in the sulcular stroma, suggestive of a role in epithelial maintenance.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from spatial mapping with interpretation.

claims.claim: Ligand-receptor analysis predicted RSPO1, CLEC11A, and FLRT2 as top ranked ligands expressed by Fb2 based on target genes expressed by epithelial cells.
claims.source: To further understand this, we investigated how this population and epithelial cells interact with each other by using a ligand–receptor pipeline (Browaeys et al., 2020); this analysis predicted RSPO1, CLEC11A, and FLRT2 as top ranked ligands expressed by Fb2 based on target genes expressed by epithelial cells (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from NicheNet ligand-receptor analysis.

claims.claim: In human oral mucosa, Fb2 fibroblasts may be required for epithelial niche maintenance.
claims.source: Thus, in human oral mucosa, Fb2 fibroblasts may be required for epithelial niche maintenance.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the spatial location and ligand expression of Fb2.

claims.claim: Both fibroblasts 4 and 5 localised in immune enriched areas, which confirmed their potential role in immune regulation.
claims.source: Both fibroblasts 4 and 5 localised in immune enriched areas, which confirmed their potential role in immune regulation with enrichment for various cytokine-mediated signalling pathways, IFNγ signalling, and pathways involved in T-cell activation (Figure 6A and E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from spatial mapping and GO enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: Fibroblasts 4 and 5 show enrichment for various cytokine-mediated signalling pathways, IFNγ signalling, and pathways involved in T-cell activation.
claims.source: Both fibroblasts 4 and 5 localised in immune enriched areas, which confirmed their potential role in immune regulation with enrichment for various cytokine-mediated signalling pathways, IFNγ signalling, and pathways involved in T-cell activation (Figure 6A and E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from GO enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: Location-specific transcriptional programmes reflect the individual functional requirements of the surrounding tissue and are imprinted during development by epigenetic regulation of HOX genes.
claims.source: Overall, these results follow previous evidence of location-specific transcriptional programmes that reflect the individual functional requirements of the surrounding tissue, and which were shown to be imprinted during development by epigenetic regulation of HOX genes (Frank-Bertoncelj et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a statement connecting the findings to prior research, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Fibroblast 5 represented a rare cell population (<1%) in the reference dataset.
claims.source: Thus, we focused on fibroblast 5, which represented a rare cell population (<1%) in our reference dataset, and which was found markedly increased in disease and barely detected in healthy patients (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq reference dataset.

claims.claim: Fibroblast 5 was found markedly increased in disease and barely detected in healthy patients.
claims.source: Thus, we focused on fibroblast 5, which represented a rare cell population (<1%) in our reference dataset, and which was found markedly increased in disease and barely detected in healthy patients (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from comparing health and disease samples.

claims.claim: Fibroblast 5 was mainly located in regions that co-localised with other immune cell types.
claims.source: These fibroblasts were mainly located in regions that co-localised with other immune cell types, and are characterised by expression of RAC2, LCP1, and TNFRS11B, a negative regulator of bone resorption and key regulator of osteoclast activity as previously described (Figure 6B–E).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from spatial mapping.

claims.claim: Fibroblast 5 is characterised by expression of RAC2, LCP1, and TNFRS11B.
claims.source: These fibroblasts were mainly located in regions that co-localised with other immune cell types, and are characterised by expression of RAC2, LCP1, and TNFRS11B, a negative regulator of bone resorption and key regulator of osteoclast activity as previously described (Figure 6B–E).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis.

claims.claim: TNFRS11B is a negative regulator of bone resorption and key regulator of osteoclast activity.
claims.source: These fibroblasts were mainly located in regions that co-localised with other immune cell types, and are characterised by expression of RAC2, LCP1, and TNFRS11B, a negative regulator of bone resorption and key regulator of osteoclast activity as previously described (Figure 6B–E).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about TNFRS11B function.

claims.claim: Fibroblast 5 shows enrichment of genes involved in 'cytokine production', 'immune response', and 'T-cell activation'.
claims.source: Overall, this population shows enrichment of genes involved in 'cytokine production', 'immune response', and 'T-cell activation' (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from GO enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: Fibroblast 5 shows a higher expression of chemokines such as CXCL8 and CXCL10, and ALOX5AP.

results.result: Spatial transcriptomics of healthy human oral mucosa identified 4-10 anatomical compartments per slide with distinct molecular signatures. The lamina propria showed functional specialization with subepithelial regions enriched for epithelial development genes and reticular regions enriched for ECM organization genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C30 describe the spatial transcriptomics methodology, technical validation with replicates (C20), sequencing depth (C21), and identification of anatomical compartments (C22, C26-C30). The use of BayesSpace for deconvolution (C24-C25) and GO enrichment analysis (C29-C30) provide computational validation. The findings are supported by figures and consistent with prior knowledge about tissue organization (C26, C31).

results.result: Spatial transcriptomics of diseased oral mucosa revealed pro-inflammatory tissue remodeling with upregulation of inflammatory gene signatures and vascular morphogenesis genes (CXCL12, CLDN5, TAGLN) in the stromal compartment.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C37 describe spatial transcriptomics analysis of disease samples showing pro-inflammatory changes validated by IHC (C35). The findings of stromal upregulation of inflammatory and vascular genes are supported by differential expression analysis with figure references. The interpretation that tissue-specific properties reflect local organization (C38) is a reasonable inference from the spatial patterns observed.

results.result: Periodontitis risk genes CDKN2B, IL1A, IL1B, and VAMP8 showed restricted expression in the junctional epithelium, suggesting that junctional epithelium dysfunction is a major driver of periodontitis pathogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C39 and C117 report spatial localization of GWAS risk genes to the junctional epithelium. While the spatial mapping data (C39) is supported, the causal interpretation that junctional epithelium dysfunction 'underlies' or is a 'major driver' of pathogenesis (C40, C117) is speculative. The spatial correlation of risk genes does not establish causality or mechanism, and no functional validation is provided.

results.result: The three anatomical regions of gingival epithelium (oral, sulcular, and junctional) were distinguished by distinct transcriptional signatures. SOX9 showed restricted expression to the junctional epithelium and may label stem cell/progenitor populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C48 describe the molecular characterization of the three epithelial regions with distinct keratin signatures and GO enrichment patterns, supported by spatial mapping data. The observation of SOX9 expression in junctional epithelium (C49) is data-supported, though the hypothesis that it labels stem cells (C51) is appropriately qualified as speculation based on its known role in other tissues (C50). The characterization of the basal layer (C52) is also data-supported.

results.result: A rare disease-associated proliferative epithelial population characterized by TOP2A and CENPF expression was identified, with TOP2A expression restricted to the junctional epithelium and significantly increased in disease, suggesting that inflammatory environments regulate stem cell behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 describe identification and spatial mapping of a proliferative population with increased expression in disease, which is data-supported. However, the interpretation that inflammatory environments 'lead to' increased proliferation (C56) and 'may regulate stem cell behaviour' (C57) is speculative. The causal relationship is not established, and no mechanistic experiments or lineage tracing are provided to support the stem cell regulation hypothesis.

results.result: Distinct stromal regions adjacent to different epithelial compartments showed specialized functions, with the junctional epithelium stroma enriched for neutrophil activation genes and the sulcular stroma enriched for angiogenesis genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 describe spatial clustering of stromal regions adjacent to epithelial compartments with distinct GO enrichment patterns. The findings are supported by spatial mapping and GO enrichment analysis with figure references. The interpretation that these regions play a role in epithelial specification or dysregulation (C58) is a reasonable inference from the spatial organization.

results.result: Cell-cell communication analysis revealed that in health, dominant interactions occur between epithelial layers (MMP9-LRP1, ADAM17-NOTCH1), while in disease, stromal-immune-endothelial interactions emerge, particularly in reticular regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C64 describe specific ligand-receptor interactions identified using Giotto spatial neighborhood analysis, with clear differences between health and disease. The interpretation that stromal/immune/endothelial interactions dominate in disease while structural interactions shape healthy tissue physiology (C65) is supported by the network analysis data with figure references.

results.result: Integration of scRNA-seq with spatial transcriptomics enabled mapping of cell types including melanocytes, γδ T cells, and Tregs that were undetected in scRNA-seq alone. Neutrophils were successfully mapped and showed significant increase in disease, confirming prior flow cytometry findings.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C73 and C76 describe the integration methodology and successful mapping of various cell types, including those missed by scRNA-seq alone. The detection of endothelial cells (C70), rare immune populations (C71), and neutrophils (C76) demonstrates the complementary value of spatial transcriptomics. The neutrophil findings confirm prior flow cytometry results (C74-C76), providing orthogonal validation.

results.result: Five fibroblast subtypes showed distinct spatial enrichment patterns. Fibroblast 2 (GREM1+, SFRP1+) was enriched in subepithelial regions and expressed ligands (RSPO1, CLEC11A, FLRT2) predicted to interact with epithelial cells, suggesting a role in epithelial niche maintenance.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C83 describe spatial mapping of fibroblast subtypes using BayesSpace and identification of Fb2 enrichment in subepithelial regions with specific ligand expression from NicheNet analysis. The hypothesis that Fb2 is required for epithelial niche maintenance (C84) is appropriately qualified as speculation but is supported by the spatial location, ligand expression data, and comparison to similar populations in other tissues (C131).

results.result: A rare pathogenic fibroblast population (Fb5, <1% in health) was identified that is markedly increased in disease, co-localizes with immune cells, and expresses chemokines CXCL8 and CXCL10 along with ALOX5AP. Multiplex ISH validated the spatial distribution and co-localization with macrophages and B cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C96 describe the identification, characterization, and spatial mapping of Fb5, supported by scRNA-seq abundance data (C88-C89), spatial mapping (C90), marker gene expression (C91, C93-C94), and spatial co-localization with chemokines and immune cells (C96). The validation by multiplex ISH (C103-C105) provides orthogonal confirmation of the spatial transcriptomics findings. The data supporting this rare population is robust across multiple modalities.

results.result: The chemokines and enzymes expressed by Fb5 have established roles in immune cell recruitment and angiogenesis. CXCL8 mediates neutrophil recruitment and angiogenesis, CXCL10 recruits leukocytes and regulates immune responses, and ALOX5AP controls leukotriene production and blood progenitor formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C102 and C134-C139 describe the known biological functions of CXCL8, CXCL10, and ALOX5AP, all supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These claims provide biological context for interpreting the expression of these genes by Fb5, though they do not directly test the function of Fb5 in this tissue.

results.result: Fibroblast 5 is hypothesized to facilitate the transition from innate to adaptive immunity by recruiting and maintaining lymphocyte populations through irregular chemokine gradients, contributing to persistent inflammation in periodontitis.
results.evaluation: Claims C106, C141-C144 present hypotheses about Fb5 function based on its spatial location, gene expression, and comparison to other chronic inflammatory diseases. While the spatial and expression data are supported, the mechanistic claims about chemokine gradients (C142), transition between immune responses (C143), and inability to return to homeostasis (C144) are speculative and lack direct experimental validation. These are reasonable hypotheses but require functional studies for confirmation.

results.result: The study provides the first molecular mapping of the three distinct epithelia composing masticatory mucosa and demonstrates that the lamina propria is organized into specialized compartments for epithelial maintenance, ECM remodeling, and immune regulation, with region-specific stromal signatures.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C111 summarize the major findings about tissue organization. The claim of providing the 'first molecular mapping' (C110) is a novelty claim that cannot be fully verified without comprehensive literature review, but the spatial transcriptomics data supporting the functional compartmentalization (C107-C109, C111) is well-supported by the GO enrichment and spatial mapping analyses throughout the manuscript.

results.result: A candidate cell-cell communication network was constructed showing emergence of a stromal-immune-endothelial axis in disease with increased WNT receptor expression in basal-subepithelial interactions, while healthy tissue showed increased ADAM17-NOTCH1 interactions between basal and suprabasal epithelial cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C120 describe findings from the Giotto cell-cell communication analysis, identifying specific interaction patterns that differ between health and disease. These findings are supported by the spatial neighborhood network analysis with appropriate figure references and represent a data-driven characterization of the communication landscape.

results.result: Background claims establish that oral mucosa is a complex, heterogeneous tissue with distinct anatomical regions and functional properties, and that spatial transcriptomics can overcome limitations of traditional approaches to study tissue organization and cell-cell communication.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C16 provide background context about oral mucosa anatomy, function, disease associations, and the rationale for using spatial transcriptomics. These are either established anatomical knowledge (C1-C5, C10, C14) or supported by appropriate citations to the literature (C6-C9, C11, C16). They provide necessary context but are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: Discussion claims contextualize findings within existing knowledge about tissue organization, stem cells, fibroblasts, and chronic inflammatory disease, noting limitations of prior approaches and comparisons to other tissues and diseases.
results.evaluation: Claims C31, C50, C92, C95, C112-C116, C121-C129, C131, C145-C149 provide context from the literature about related findings in other tissues, limitations of prior methods, and conceptual frameworks for interpreting the results. These are appropriately supported by citations and represent accurate characterization of the field, though they are not novel findings of this study.
